Short Answer Questions on Medical Vectors

snip.t: Glossina = tsetse fly (African trypanosomiasis); Simulium = onchocerciasis; Ixodes = Lyme disease.

qs.q: Which characteristic cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) finding is expected in Stage II African trypanosomiasis with CNS involvement?
o: Decreased intracranial pressure and leukopenia are observed
Normal protein levels and hypoglycemia are observed
Clear fluid with isolated neutrophilic predominance shown
Raised intracranial pressure, pleocytosis, and raised protein
qs.e: Stage II sleeping sickness causes chronic meningoencephalitis leading to raised intracranial pressure, increased WBCs (pleocytosis), and raised protein levels in the CSF. Normal protein levels would contradict active CNS infection.

qs.q: Which stage II treatment for African trypanosomiasis is known to cross the blood-brain barrier and is used for T.b. rhodesiense CNS infection?
qs.e: Melarsoprol crosses the blood-brain barrier and is utilized for Stage II T.b. rhodesiense infections. Suramin is restricted to Stage I because it does not cross the barrier.

qs.q: What is a characteristic histopathological feature found in the meninges during Stage II African trypanosomiasis?
o: Presence of Negri bodies in neurons
Presence of morula cells containing IgA
Presence of Aschoff bodies near vessels
qs.e: Histopathology of Stage II sleeping sickness reveals chronic meningoencephalitis with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and morula cells, which contain mulberry-shaped IgA masses. Negri bodies are characteristic of rabies rather than trypanosomiasis.

qs.q: Which laboratory finding is considered a non-specific indicator of African trypanosomiasis due to increased gamma globulins?
qs.e: A raised ESR occurs due to increased gamma globulins in the blood. A decreased total protein or thrombocytosis are not listed as typical non-specific findings for this condition.

qs.q: A 34-year-old traveler returning from Central Africa is diagnosed with early-stage African trypanosomiasis without central nervous system involvement. Treatment is initiated with a medication that requires intravenous infusion and carries a significant risk of renal toxicity and lack of central nervous system penetration. Which drug was most likely administered?
qs.e: Suramin is nephrotoxic and poorly crosses the blood-brain barrier, making it suitable only for the hemolymphatic stage of African trypanosomiasis. Melarsoprol crosses the blood-brain barrier but is used for late-stage disease with central nervous system involvement.

qs.q: Which preventive measure is specifically emphasized for controlling Chagas disease compared to African trypanosomiasis?
o: Mass screening for Glossina species vectors
Using insect repellents against tsetse flies
Improving housing to reduce vector entry
qs.e: Improving housing conditions and using insecticides target reduviid bugs for Chagas disease prevention. Clearing vegetation and repelling tsetse flies are meant for African trypanosomiasis control.

qs.q: What imaging modality is useful for detecting cerebral edema associated with African trypanosomiasis?
qs.e: CT imaging is utilized to identify cerebral edema, while MRI is used for white matter enhancement in African trypanosomiasis. X-rays and ultrasound are not used for brain pathology.

qs.q: Which of the following blood smear stains is explicitly recommended for identifying parasites such as malaria, trypanosomiasis, and babesiosis?
qs.e: Blood smears with Giemsa or Wright stain are utilized to identify blood-borne parasites. Gram stain is generally used for bacterial identification.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Trypanosomiasis is a protozoal infection transmitted by tsetse flies (African) or triatomine bugs (American). It causes systemic illness that can progress to severe neurological disease if untreated.

sections.p: Trypanosomiasis refers to infection with Trypanosoma species. Diagnosis relies on detecting parasites in blood, lymph, CSF, or tissue, and on serology for chronic disease.
b: Microscopy of wet prep or concentration methods
Serologic ELISA or rapid test for T. cruzi
PCR when available for species identification

sections.p: African disease is staged by CNS involvement: Stage 1 (hemolymphatic) vs Stage 2 (meningo‑encephalitic). American disease is acute vs chronic (cardiac/gastrointestinal).
b: Stage 1: parasites in blood/lymph, no CSF abnormalities
Stage 2: parasites in CSF, raised white cells, protein

sections.p: In endemic areas, the most common cause is vector‑borne infection with T. brucei gambiense (West Africa) or T. brucei rhodesiense (East Africa). In the Americas, T. cruzi from triatomine bugs is predominant.
b: T. brucei gambiense – chronic, low parasitemia
T. brucei rhodesiense – acute, high parasitemia
T. cruzi – oral, congenital, transfusion

sections.p: Early disease shows fever, headache, lymphadenopathy, and a chancre at the bite site. Later, sleep disturbance, neuropsychiatric changes, and motor signs appear in African disease; cardiac arrhythmia or megacolon appear in chronic Chagas.
b: Fever, malaise, arthralgia
Sleep cycle disruption (African)
Cardiomyopathy, megaviscera (American)

sections.p: Laboratory and imaging confirm infection and assess organ involvement.

t.b: Does the patient have circulating trypomastigotes? Positive confirms active infection.
Is there CNS involvement? Elevated white cells (>5/µL) or protein indicates Stage 2 African disease.
Is there chronic exposure to T. cruzi? Positive in chronic Chagas when parasites are scarce.
Which Trypanosoma species is present? Helpful for treatment choice when microscopy is negative.
Is there cardiac involvement in Chagas? Detects arrhythmias, conduction blocks, or ventricular dysfunction.

sections.p: Unchecked disease can lead to irreversible organ damage and death.
b: Severe sleep disruption with coma (African)
Heart failure or sudden arrhythmia (American)
Severe weight loss, cachexia

sections.p: Treat the parasite first, then address organ dysfunction. Drug choice depends on species and disease stage.
b: Pentamidine for early West African disease; avoids severe toxicity of melarsoprol
Suramin for early East African disease; renal monitoring required
Eflornithine (often with nifurtimox) for Stage 2 West African disease; crosses blood‑brain barrier
Benznidazole or nifurtimox for chronic Chagas; chosen for efficacy and oral administration

sections.p: Regular monitoring for relapse and organ damage is essential; vector control reduces new cases.
b: Repeat blood smears at 3‑month intervals until negative
Annual ECG for Chagas patients
Use insecticide‑treated nets, screen blood donors, and treat animal reservoirs

sections.p: Several tropical infections share similar early features.
b: Malaria (fever, parasitemia)
Leishmaniasis (cutaneous lesions, fever)
Tuberculosis (weight loss, night sweats)

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely negative or misleading in low‑resource settings.
b: Blood smear may miss low‑level parasitemia; consider concentration techniques
Serology can stay positive after cure; interpret with clinical context
PCR unavailable in many clinics; rely on clinical staging

whenToSeekHelp: Severe cardiac arrhythmia or heart failure

faq.a: Yes, early treatment clears parasites; chronic cardiac disease may persist despite cure.

faq.q: Why is melarsoprol rarely used now?
faq.a: It is highly neurotoxic and can cause fatal encephalopathy, so safer alternatives are preferred.
No vaccine exists; prevention relies on vector control and screening of blood products.

exam: Describe the diagnostic criteria that separate Stage 1 from Stage 2 African trypanosomiasis.
List the first‑line drug for early West African disease and explain why melarsoprol is avoided.
Explain the major cardiac complications of chronic Chagas disease and how they are monitored.
